NHS Provider Sector.description: The 206 NHS trusts that actually deliver care across England — hospitals, mental-health, community, specialist, and ambulance services. Collectively employ ~1.35 million FTE and run ~163,000 beds. Their funding flows from NHS England via the 42 Integrated Care Boards (ICBs) that replaced 106 CCGs in July 2022.
NHS Provider Sector.beneficiaries: 56.5 million people registered with an NHS GP in England — free at point of use
NHS Provider Sector.legal_basis: NHS Act 2006, as amended by the Health and Social Care Act 2012 and Health and Care Act 2022
NHS Provider Sector.notes: Elective waiting list peaked at 7.77M (Sept 2023) — the defining political issue. Sector moved from ~£1.4B underlying deficit (2022-23) to a planned ~£2.2B deficit for 2024-25; ~60% of trusts in deficit at year-end 2023-24. Provider workforce grew ~20% since 2019 but productivity remains below pre-pandemic (Health Foundation).

NHS Acute Trusts.description: The ~130 hospital trusts running district general and teaching hospitals — A&E, surgery, maternity, inpatient medicine, elective care. The largest slice of provider spending by far, and where the elective waiting list accumulates.
NHS Acute Trusts.beneficiaries: Every England resident uses an acute trust for emergency or elective care; trust populations range 250k–1.5M
NHS Acute Trusts.legal_basis: NHS Act 2006, Part 2 (NHS Trusts) and Chapter 5 (Foundation Trusts)

key_stats.label: Top teaching trusts
key_stats.value: Barts · Manchester · Guy's & St Thomas' · UHB · Leeds

NHS Acute Trusts.notes: RAAC crisis: seven hospitals structurally unsafe due to reinforced autoclaved aerated concrete; the New Hospital Programme delayed to mid-2030s (NAO 2023). 78-week waits largely eliminated by 2024 but 65-week target missed. Activity still 5–8% below pre-pandemic on some measures despite higher staffing.

NHS Mental Health Trusts.description: ~50 specialist trusts providing inpatient psychiatric beds, community mental-health teams, crisis services, CAMHS (children & young people), and learning-disability services. Many are combined MH + community trusts serving defined geographies.
NHS Mental Health Trusts.beneficiaries: ~3.8 million people in contact with NHS mental-health services (2023-24); ~1.2M referrals to CYP services
NHS Mental Health Trusts.legal_basis: Mental Health Act 1983 (as amended 2007); Mental Capacity Act 2005; NHS Act 2006
NHS Mental Health Trusts.notes: MH Investment Standard requires ICBs to grow MH spend faster than overall NHS allocation. CYP referrals up ~50% since 2019. Edenfield Centre and Greater Manchester MH FT abuse scandals (2022-23) triggered a Rapid Review. Inappropriate out-of-area placements and use of private locked-rehab beds remain acute.

NHS Community Trusts.description: Trusts delivering care outside hospital walls — district nursing, health visiting, school nursing, community hospitals, intermediate care, musculoskeletal services, community paediatrics, and increasingly virtual wards. Often combined with MH services.
NHS Community Trusts.beneficiaries: ~8–10 million community-service contacts per year; district nursing alone sees ~2.6M people
NHS Community Trusts.legal_basis: NHS Act 2006; Health & Care Act 2022 (ICB commissioning)
NHS Community Trusts.notes: The 'Cinderella service' — repeatedly flagged by the King's Fund for data invisibility and workforce shortages. Health-visitor FTE down 40% since 2015. Transforming Community Services (post-2009) separated community from PCTs into standalone trusts or 'vertical integration' with acutes. Virtual wards scaled rapidly 2022-24 as alternative to admission.

NHS Ambulance Trusts.description: Ten regional trusts running 999 emergency response, NHS 111, patient transport, and hazardous-area response across England. Operate the Category 1–4 response model with nationally-set response-time targets.
NHS Ambulance Trusts.beneficiaries: All 56.5M England residents; ~14M 999 calls and ~20M NHS 111 contacts per year
NHS Ambulance Trusts.legal_basis: NHS Act 2006; ambulance trusts established under s.25

key_stats.label: Trusts
key_stats.value: 10 (LAS, SCAS, SECamb, SWAST, WMAS, EMAS, EEAST, YAS, NWAS, NEAS)

NHS Ambulance Trusts.notes: Category 2 performance collapsed winter 2022-23 due to hospital handover delays (crews stuck outside A&E). £150M+ additional funding and '45-min handover rule' introduced 2023-24. AACE estimated ~57,000 patients harmed in 2022 by delays; criminal investigation at some trusts re crew conduct and patient deaths.

Local Government (England).description: The sum of revenue spending by England's 317 principal councils plus police & crime commissioners, fire authorities, combined authorities and parish precepts. Covers everything from adult social care and schools through to bin collection, libraries, planning and housing-benefit administration.
Local Government (England).beneficiaries: 57 million people in England — every resident is covered by 1-2 tiers of council
Local Government (England).legal_basis: Local Government Act 1972 (structure); Local Government Finance Act 1988 (business rates) & 1992 (council tax); Localism Act 2011 (general power of competence)

key_stats.label: Central grants
key_stats.value: ~27% (Social Care Grant, Better Care Fund, PH, RSG)

key_stats.label: Biggest service line
key_stats.value: Adult Social Care (~£23B net, 40%+ of council budgets)

Local Government (England).notes: Core Spending Power rose ~6.5% YoY 2024-25 but real-terms funding down ~10% since 2010. Eight s114 notices issued 2018-2024. Birmingham (Sept 2023, £760M equal-pay liability + Oracle ERP disaster) was the biggest council bankruptcy in UK history. Thurrock £1.5B solar-farm losses (2022), Woking £1.2B debt (2023), Nottingham's Robin Hood Energy collapse have become totems of commercial over-reach.

sources.title: Local Authority Revenue Expenditure and Financing 2023-24 (RO5)
How have councils' funding and spending changed? (2024)

London Boroughs.description: 32 London boroughs plus the City of London Corporation — all single-tier councils, but share strategic functions (transport, fire, policing, economic development) with the GLA and Mayor of London. A unique hybrid of unitary and two-tier.
London Boroughs.beneficiaries: 8.9 million London residents; average ~270k per borough
London Boroughs.legal_basis: London Government Act 1963; Greater London Authority Act 1999
London Boroughs.notes: Temporary-accommodation cost explosion — London boroughs spent £4M/day on TA in 2024, up 68% in two years (London Councils). Croydon issued three s114 notices (2020, 2020, 2022) after its Brick-by-Brick housing vehicle collapsed with £200M+ losses. Westminster & Wandsworth maintain historic low-band-D discount that pre-dates the modern funding formula.

sources.title: Council Tax Levels Set by Local Authorities in England 2024-25

Shire Counties.description: Upper-tier authorities in the surviving two-tier areas — Kent, Essex, Hampshire, Surrey, Hertfordshire, Lancashire and 15 others. Deliver the expensive people-services (social care, schools, roads, fire in some areas) while shire districts below them do housing, bins and planning.
Shire Counties.beneficiaries: ~26M people across ~47% of England's land area
Shire Counties.legal_basis: Local Government Act 1972 (two-tier model); Children Act 1989; Care Act 2014
Shire Counties.notes: County Councils Network reports counties face £54B adult-social-care bill by 2030. Average county raised council tax by the maximum 4.99% without referendum every year 2022-25. Surrey CC abandoned its 15% referendum in 2017 under government pressure. Hampshire, Kent and Hertfordshire all issued effective-bankruptcy warnings in 2024.

sources.title: State of Local Government Finance Survey 2024

Metropolitan Districts.description: The 36 single-tier 'met borough' councils covering the six former metropolitan county areas — Greater Manchester (10), Merseyside (5), South Yorkshire (4), Tyne & Wear (5), West Midlands (7), West Yorkshire (5). Include Birmingham, Leeds, Manchester, Liverpool, Sheffield, Newcastle.
Metropolitan Districts.beneficiaries: ~12 million residents in England's largest conurbations outside London
Metropolitan Districts.legal_basis: Local Government Acts 1972 & 1985 (which abolished the Met County Councils, leaving districts unitary); Cities and Local Government Devolution Act 2016

key_stats.label: Largest
key_stats.value: Birmingham (1.15M — largest single council in Europe)

Metropolitan Districts.notes: Now nest inside mayoral Combined Authorities (GMCA, WMCA, WYCA, SYMCA, LCR, NECA, Tees Valley) which retain business-rate growth and receive devolved settlements (~£1B GMCA 2024-25). Birmingham s114 Sept 2023 was the biggest council bankruptcy in UK history — £760M equal-pay liability + £131M Oracle implementation failure — leading to a 21% council-tax rise and £300M asset fire-sale.

sources.title: Local government finance in a time of COVID-19 (2024 update)

Unitary Authorities.description: Single-tier councils outside London and the met areas that combine county and district functions. Created in successive waves — 1990s (46), 2009 (9), and 2019-2023 (a new wave of mergers that collapsed 40+ councils into larger unitaries).
Unitary Authorities.legal_basis: Local Government Act 1992 (LGR Commission); Local Government and Public Involvement in Health Act 2007 (2009 wave); Structural Changes Orders under that Act (2019-23 wave)

key_stats.label: 2019-23 merger wave
key_stats.value: Bucks · Dorset · Somerset · North Yorkshire · Cumbria

Unitary Authorities.notes: The 2019-23 merger wave: Buckinghamshire (2020), Dorset + BCP (2019), Somerset (2023), North Yorkshire (2023), Cumberland + Westmorland-and-Furness (2023) — projected £20-40M annual savings each, though realisation disputed. Woking BC issued s114 in June 2023 with £1.2B debt (18× revenue) from commercial property + a Victoria Square development; government now forcing reorganisation into a Surrey unitary. Slough s114 (2021) after £760M accounting hole.

Shire Districts.description: The 164 lower-tier district and borough councils in two-tier areas — the 'bins and benches' tier. Deliver housing, planning, waste collection (not disposal), leisure, licensing, environmental health, council-tax collection and housing-benefit administration.
Shire Districts.legal_basis: Local Government Act 1972; Housing Act 1996 (homelessness duty); Town and Country Planning Act 1990
Shire Districts.notes: Homelessness / TA costs up 60%+ since 2020 for many districts. District Councils Network reports a quarter of districts risk s114 by 2026 without reform. Government's 2024 local-audit crisis hit districts hardest (backlog of 900+ unaudited accounts). Thurrock (£1.5B solar-bond losses 2022) was the largest commercial-investment failure in local-government history.

sources.title: Timeliness of local auditor reporting on local government in England (2024)

Other Authorities.description: Everything outside the principal councils — 43 territorial police forces (funded via PCCs or mayors), ~30 fire & rescue authorities, the Greater London Authority, 10+ Mayoral Combined Authorities, ~9,000 parishes, plus national park authorities and integrated transport authorities.
Other Authorities.beneficiaries: All England residents — every household pays a policing precept and fire precept on top of council tax
Other Authorities.legal_basis: Police Reform and Social Responsibility Act 2011 (PCCs); Fire and Rescue Services Act 2004; Greater London Authority Act 1999; Cities and Local Government Devolution Act 2016; Levelling-up and Regeneration Act 2023

key_stats.label: Mayoral Combined Authorities
key_stats.value: 10+ (GM, WM, WYCA, SYMCA, LCR, NECA, Tees Valley, East Midlands, York & N.Yorks)

Other Authorities.notes: Four English mayors gained 'trailblazer' single-settlement status (GM & WM in 2024; North East, Liverpool, South Yorkshire in 2025). Police precepts up £13 Band D flexibility 2024-25. PCC model criticised for low turnout (15–25% at elections). Parish precepts uncapped — Queen's Park Community Council and some town councils raising 40%+ to fund services districts have cut.

State Pension.description: Contributory pension paid to individuals who have reached State Pension age with sufficient NI contributions. Two systems run in parallel: the 'new' State Pension (for those reaching pension age after 6 April 2016, full rate £221.20/week) and the 'basic' State Pension (for earlier cohorts, £169.50/week plus additional SERPS/S2P).
State Pension.legal_basis: Pensions Act 2014 (new State Pension); Social Security Contributions and Benefits Act 1992 (basic/additional)
State Pension.notes: WASPI — 1950s-born women had their State Pension age raised from 60 to 66 with inadequate notice. PHSO recommended £1,000–£2,950 compensation each (March 2024) for ~3.6M affected women. Government rejected the scheme in December 2024, sparking ongoing backlash. The triple lock itself — guaranteeing annual uprating by the highest of CPI, earnings, or 2.5% — cost DWP an extra ~£9B in the April 2024 uprating.

Universal Credit.description: Means-tested benefit for working-age people on low income, merging six legacy benefits (Income Support, income-based JSA, income-related ESA, Housing Benefit, Child Tax Credit, Working Tax Credit) into one monthly payment with a single taper rate.
Universal Credit.beneficiaries: 6.9 million people on UC (Aug 2024) — ~3.2M households with children · ~38% in work · 58% female lead claimants
Universal Credit.legal_basis: Welfare Reform Act 2012; Universal Credit Regulations 2013
Universal Credit.notes: Two-child limit: ~1.6M children in 450k households affected (CPAG 2024); c.£3,455/year lost per additional child. JRF estimates removing the limit would lift 540k children out of poverty for ~£3.4B. 'Managed Migration' of ~800k remaining legacy tax-credit / ESA / JSA / IS / HB claimants accelerated in 2024 — now targeted for completion by March 2026 (originally 2028). Autumn 2024 Budget confirmed a lower deduction cap of 15% (Fair Repayment Rate) from April 2025.

Personal Independence Payment.description: Non-means-tested, non-taxable payment for working-age adults (16 to State Pension age) with a long-term disability or health condition that affects daily living or mobility. Assessed via a points-based functional assessment, not the diagnosis itself.
Personal Independence Payment.beneficiaries: 3.6 million claimants in England & Wales (July 2024) — up from 2.05M in 2019. 55% female, 45% male. Under-25s ~9% of caseload but fastest-growing cohort.
Personal Independence Payment.legal_basis: Welfare Reform Act 2012, Part 4; replaced Disability Living Allowance for working-age from 2013
Personal Independence Payment.notes: ~68% of PIP appeals that reach tribunal overturn the DWP decision (MoJ Tribunal Statistics Q2 2024) — one of the highest overturn rates in the system. Mandatory Reconsideration success rate much lower (~25%). Conservative Spring 2024 Green Paper proposed replacing cash with vouchers/one-off grants — shelved. Labour's Autumn 2024 signalled tighter assessment criteria in the forthcoming 2025 welfare-reform Green Paper.

Pension Credit.description: Means-tested top-up for pensioners on the lowest incomes. Two parts: Guarantee Credit (tops income up to a weekly threshold) and Savings Credit (available only to those reaching pension age before April 2016).
Pension Credit.beneficiaries: ~1.4 million households (May 2024) — ~62% female · ~75% single claimants · concentrated in NE England, Wales, NI
Pension Credit.notes: The notorious take-up gap — only ~63% of eligible pensioners claim, leaving ~760,000 eligible households missing out on an average £2,500/year. The biggest cash-gap benefit in the UK system. Labour's July 2024 decision to means-test Winter Fuel Payment via Pension Credit drove a 152% surge in PC applications Aug–Sept 2024. Pension Credit also opens the gateway to a free TV licence (75+), Council Tax Reduction, Housing Benefit top-up, and cold-weather payments.

sources.title: Income-related benefits: estimates of take-up 2021 to 2022 (Feb 2024)

Attendance Allowance.description: Non-means-tested, tax-free disability benefit for people over State Pension age who need help with personal care or supervision. No mobility component (unlike PIP/DLA). Not affected by savings or income.
Attendance Allowance.beneficiaries: ~1.66 million claimants (May 2024) — 100% aged 65+ · ~65% female · average age ~81
Attendance Allowance.legal_basis: Social Security Contributions and Benefits Act 1992, Part III

key_stats.label: Higher rate (day AND night, or terminal)

Attendance Allowance.notes: Massive under-claim — Age UK estimates ~1.1 million eligible pensioners don't claim (~£5.2B unclaimed annually). Awareness that it is NOT means-tested is the single biggest uptake barrier — many pensioners wrongly believe savings disqualify them. 2023 HoC Work & Pensions Committee flagged AA for review given ageing caseload and overlap with PIP at pension-age cutoff.

Carer's Allowance.description: Weekly payment for people providing 35+ hours of care per week for someone who receives a qualifying disability benefit (PIP daily living, AA, or DLA middle/higher care). Taxable. The lowest of all income-replacement benefits.
Carer's Allowance.beneficiaries: ~991,000 in receipt (May 2024); ~1.4M have 'underlying entitlement' but aren't paid due to overlapping-benefit rules (mostly State Pension). 71% female.
Carer's Allowance.legal_basis: Social Security Contributions and Benefits Act 1992, Part III

key_stats.label: Caree must receive
key_stats.value: PIP daily living, AA, or DLA middle/higher care

Carer's Allowance.notes: Overpayment scandal — The Guardian (April 2024) revealed 134,800 carers owed DWP money, ~£250M in outstanding debt, many prosecuted for earning £1–£2 over the cliff-edge £151 threshold. Labour commissioned Liz Sayce independent review (reporting 2025). The cliff-edge earnings rule — lose £1 over the threshold, lose the whole £81.90 — has been called 'indefensible' by the Work & Pensions Committee (Oct 2023).

MINISTRY OF DEFENCE.description: Government department responsible for the armed forces, defence policy and the nuclear deterrent. Runs three single services (Army, Royal Navy, RAF) plus Strategic Command (joint / cyber / special forces) and the Defence Nuclear Organisation, coordinated by MoD Head Office in Whitehall.
MINISTRY OF DEFENCE.beneficiaries: UK population (security) + 138k regulars + 25k reserves + ~62k civilian staff + defence-industry workforce
MINISTRY OF DEFENCE.legal_basis: Defence Act 1842; Armed Forces Act 2006 (renewed quinquennially — next due 2026)
MINISTRY OF DEFENCE.notes: Spending rose from £45.9B (2020-21) to £71.9B (2024-25) — driven by Ukraine commitments, NATO 2% floor and nuclear-deterrent renewal. IfG and RUSI repeatedly flag a '£16.9B black hole' in the Equipment Plan (NAO, Dec 2023). The Strategic Defence Review (June 2025) recommended restoring Army warfighting mass but provided no fully-funded growth path.

HM REVENUE AND CUSTOMS.description: Non-ministerial department that collects taxes, pays Child Benefit and (residual) tax credits, enforces the National Minimum Wage, and runs customs at the border. Reports to HM Treasury ministers.
HM REVENUE AND CUSTOMS.beneficiaries: All UK taxpayers (~32M individuals paying income tax); ~7M families receiving Child Benefit
HM REVENUE AND CUSTOMS.legal_basis: Commissioners for Revenue and Customs Act 2005 (merged Inland Revenue + HM Customs & Excise, 2005); Taxes Management Act 1970
HM REVENUE AND CUSTOMS.notes: Phone service collapsed 2023-24 — average wait >25 minutes; NAO called it 'unacceptable' (May 2024). Extra 5,000 compliance staff funded in the Spring Budget 2024. Tax gap at 4.8% of theoretical liability (£39.8B 2022-23) — up from 4.6%. Loan Charge (disguised remuneration) affecting ~50,000 contractors remains under independent review; APPG links 10+ suicides to HMRC enforcement action.

Child Benefit.description: Non-means-tested payment to the main carer for each child under 16 (or under 20 in approved education), administered by HMRC since 2003. Was universal until 2013, when the High Income Child Benefit Charge (HICBC) introduced clawback at upper incomes.
Child Benefit.beneficiaries: 6.92 million children in 7.66M recipient families (Aug 2024). ~88% of recipients are mothers.
Child Benefit.legal_basis: Child Benefit Act 2005; HICBC under Finance Act 2012 s.8 and Schedule 1

key_stats.label: Opted out of payment (kept NI credits)

Child Benefit.notes: HICBC is still assessed on the higher individual earner, not household income — a £70k + £0 couple loses half their CB; a £59k + £59k couple (£118k household) loses nothing. Government committed to move HICBC to household basis 'by April 2026' in March 2024 Budget, then abandoned that plan in April 2024 citing cost & complexity. Non-claiming to avoid HICBC can cost mothers NI credits (State Pension) — ~200,000 families estimated to have lost pension entitlement.

SCOTTISH GOVERNMENT.description: Scotland's devolved administration, funded mainly by the Barnett-formula block grant from HMT plus revenues from devolved taxes (Scottish Rates of Income Tax since 2017, Land & Buildings Transaction Tax replacing Stamp Duty). Runs NHS Scotland, schools, councils, transport, police and justice.
SCOTTISH GOVERNMENT.beneficiaries: 5.48 million Scottish residents — free at point of use for devolved services
SCOTTISH GOVERNMENT.legal_basis: Scotland Act 1998 (as amended by Scotland Acts 2012 and 2016); Fiscal Framework 2016 (renewed 2023)

key_stats.label: Scotland Act revenue powers
key_stats.value: 100% of Scottish Income Tax · LBTT · Landfill · (ADT dormant)

SCOTTISH GOVERNMENT.notes: The Fiscal Framework uses the 'Indexed Per Capita' (IPC) method for Block Grant Adjustments — the deduction grows with rUK revenue per head × Scottish population. Reserve drawdowns and borrowing are capped. Scotland's progressive five-band structure has widened divergence with rUK since 2017, raising an extra ~£1.5B/year from higher earners — a policy choice the SG has consistently defended despite 'tax competitiveness' critiques.

Dedicated Schools Grant (DSG).description: The main DfE ring-fenced grant to English local authorities for schools, high needs (SEND), and central services. Local authorities pass the Schools Block to maintained schools; academy trusts receive their share via ESFA recoupment. Allocated through the National Funding Formula.
Dedicated Schools Grant (DSG).beneficiaries: ~8.2 million pupils in ~22,000 state-funded schools in England · ~468,000 FTE teachers
Dedicated Schools Grant (DSG).legal_basis: School Standards and Framework Act 1998; Academies Act 2010; annual DSG Conditions of Grant
Dedicated Schools Grant (DSG).notes: Scope note: headline £59.6B covers the whole-England DSG; the tree node you're looking at may show a narrower sub-line (e.g. the part recouped from LAs for academy trusts). Core schools budget rose from ~£47B (2021-22) to £59.6B (2024-25), +27% cash. But real-terms per-pupil spend only returned to 2010 levels in 2024-25 (IFS). The NFF's 'levelling up' raised floors for historically low-funded schools but squeezed London/inner-city authorities relatively. Unions argue the 2024 teacher pay award was only partially funded by the Core Schools Budget Grant.

sources.title: Annual Report on Education Spending in England (Sibieta, 2024)

Student Loans.description: Income-contingent loans to cover tuition fees and maintenance for higher-education students, disbursed by the Student Loans Company. Repaid via PAYE once earnings exceed a threshold; unpaid balance written off after a term of years. Part counted as spending via the RAB charge.
Student Loans.beneficiaries: ~1.6 million borrowers received loans in 2023-24 · ~8.1 million people have outstanding student-loan debt
Student Loans.legal_basis: Teaching and Higher Education Act 1998; Higher Education Act 2004; Education (Student Loans) (Repayment) Regulations 2009
Student Loans.notes: Scope note: ~£20B gross annual disbursements is the cash paid TO students/universities. The OSCAR spending line typically shows the much smaller 'RAB charge' (expected write-off portion, ~27-44% of lending as budgetary impact) — not the full disbursement. Plan 5 (from Aug 2023) cut the repayment threshold from £27,295 to £25,000 and extended the term from 30 to 40 years — IFS calculated this shifts ~£2.3B/year from Treasury to graduates over their lifetime, hitting middle earners hardest. The 2018 ONS reclassification forced the write-off portion onto the deficit; Augar Review reforms partly adopted in Plan 5 were criticised as regressive — lowest earners pay more, highest earners pay less.

sources.title: Student Loans in England: Financial Year 2023-24 (June 2024)

Pupil Premium.description: Top-up grant paid to English schools for disadvantaged pupils — designed to narrow the attainment gap. Eligibility: pupils registered for Free School Meals at any point in the last 6 years ('Ever 6 FSM'), looked-after and previously looked-after children, and service children.
Pupil Premium.beneficiaries: ~2.05 million pupils in 2024-25 — roughly 24% of state-school pupils
Pupil Premium.legal_basis: Non-statutory grant paid under s.14 Education Act 2002; schools must publish a Pupil Premium Strategy Statement
Pupil Premium.notes: Rates rose only ~1.5% for 2024-25 despite ~6% wage inflation — real-terms cut. Sutton Trust and EEF research show the disadvantage gap widened post-pandemic to the highest level in a decade. Critics argue the 'Ever 6' metric misses families just above the FSM threshold (~£7,400 household income cap). Pupil Premium has lost ~20% real value since 2015.

sources.title: Pupil premium: allocations and conditions of grant 2024-25

High Speed 2 (HS2) Construction Programm.description: High-speed rail line, originally planned as a Y-shape London–Birmingham–Manchester–Leeds. After PM Sunak's October 2023 cancellation of Phase 2, only Phase 1 (London–Birmingham) survives. Delivered by HS2 Ltd, a DfT-owned company.
High Speed 2 (HS2) Construction Programm.beneficiaries: Future rail passengers (London–Birmingham ~49 min), West Midlands economy, construction consortia, ~30,000 jobs at peak
High Speed 2 (HS2) Construction Programm.legal_basis: High Speed Rail (London–West Midlands) Act 2017 (hybrid bill); HS2 Phase 2a Act 2021 (now moribund)

key_stats.label: Euston terminus
key_stats.value: Currently unfunded — trains terminate at Old Oak Common

High Speed 2 (HS2) Construction Programm.notes: October 2023 Phase 2 cancellation scrapped Birmingham–Manchester and eastern leg; £36B redirected to 'Network North' (largely unspecified road/bus schemes). Phase 1 ≈ £470M per mile — among the most expensive railways ever built per km globally (French LGV ~£25M/km). PAC (Feb 2024) called HS2 'a casebook example of how not to run a major project'. The Chiltern tunnel cost ~£1.3B for 10 miles; the bat tunnel at Sheephouse Wood (£100M, required by Natural England) became symbolic of cost overruns.

sources.title: HS2: Update following cancellation of Phase 2 (Mar 2024)

Network Rail Government Grant.description: Grant-in-aid from DfT to Network Rail Infrastructure Ltd, which owns and operates the 20,000-mile rail network — track, signalling, 20 major stations, tunnels and bridges. Funds Network Rail's five-year Control Periods (currently CP7, 2024-29).
Network Rail Government Grant.beneficiaries: Train operating companies, 1.6 billion annual passenger journeys, freight operators, 42,000 Network Rail employees
Network Rail Government Grant.legal_basis: Railways Act 1993 (as amended); Railways Act 2005; Transport Act 2000. Reclassified as a central government body by ONS in Sept 2014, adding its debt (~£55B) to PSND
Network Rail Government Grant.notes: Labour's Passenger Railway Services (Public Ownership) Act 2024 (passed Nov 2024) ends franchising; operators return to public ownership as contracts expire (South Western Railway first, May 2025). Full Great British Railways (GBR) Bill expected 2025. Network Rail's 2014 reclassification blew a hole in fiscal rules. CP6 (2019-24) overran by billions on enhancements. Track access charges recover only ~25% of infrastructure cost; the rest is taxpayer grant.

sources.title: Rail reform: the rail transformation programme (Mar 2023)

Police Core Grant and Formula Funding.description: Main Home Office funding stream to the 43 territorial police forces in England & Wales, distributed via the Police Funding Formula. Total police funding = Home Office grant + council tax precept + specific grants. British Transport Police, Civil Nuclear Constabulary and MoD Police are separately funded.
Police Core Grant and Formula Funding.beneficiaries: 43 PCCs / Mayoral offices, ~240,000 police workforce, victims of crime
Police Core Grant and Formula Funding.legal_basis: Police Act 1996 (s.46 police grant); Police Reform and Social Responsibility Act 2011 (PCCs); annual Police Grant Report
Police Core Grant and Formula Funding.notes: Casey Review (Mar 2023) declared the Met institutionally racist, misogynistic and homophobic after Sarah Everard and David Carrick. HMICFRS placed 4 forces in 'Engage' (special measures). The officer vetting scandal — thousands of officers with concerning backgrounds retained. Funding Formula review restarted 2023 — current formula based on 2013 data, disadvantages urban forces per analyses.

Asylum System.description: Home Office system to receive, accommodate and decide asylum claims under the 1951 Refugee Convention. Includes initial accommodation, dispersed accommodation, contingency hotels, decision-making casework, appeals support, and (until July 2024) the Rwanda removal scheme.
Asylum System.beneficiaries: ~110,000 people in asylum support (Dec 2024); accommodation providers (Serco, Mears, Clearsprings); legal aid sector
Asylum System.legal_basis: Immigration and Asylum Act 1999; Nationality, Immigration and Asylum Act 2002; Nationality and Borders Act 2022; Illegal Migration Act 2023
Asylum System.notes: Rwanda scheme cancelled by Labour on 6 July 2024 (PM Starmer's second day). Total sunk cost ~£700M (£290M paid to Rwanda + £240M running costs + processing + legal fees) — zero removals occurred. Safety of Rwanda Act being repealed. Bibby Stockholm barge (Portland, Aug 2023-Nov 2024): Legionella found days after arrival; suicide of Leonard Farruku Dec 2023. Manston overcrowding Oct-Nov 2022 (4,000 in a 1,600-capacity site) led to diphtheria outbreak.

sources.title: Investigation into the costs of the UK-Rwanda Partnership (Mar 2024)

BBC Licence Fee._note: BBC Licence Fee itself is not a spending line in OSCAR 2024 (it's a levy). Aliases cover the BBC-related spending lines that do exist (FCDO World Service funding).
BBC Licence Fee.description: Compulsory annual fee payable by any household watching live TV (any channel) or using BBC iPlayer. Primary funding source for the BBC under Royal Charter. Evasion is a criminal offence punishable by fine up to £1,000.
BBC Licence Fee.beneficiaries: BBC public service output (TV, radio, online, part-funded World Service); independent production sector; S4C (statutory top-slice ~£90M)
BBC Licence Fee.legal_basis: BBC Royal Charter 2017-2027 (Article 43) and Framework Agreement; Communications Act 2003; Wireless Telegraphy Act 2006

key_stats.label: Over-75s free licence
key_stats.value: Means-tested to Pension Credit recipients since 2020

BBC Licence Fee.notes: Scope note: UK OSCAR 2024 shows only the ~£104M 'BBC World Service' transfer from FCDO — not the £3.74B licence-fee revenue (which is a household levy, not HMT spending). Figures above describe the licence-fee system for context. Charter expires 31 December 2027. DCMS launched a Funding Model Review in Nov 2024 examining alternatives (subscription, hybrid, household levy, advertising). The January 2022 freeze cost the BBC ~£285M/year real-terms. 2023 Gary Lineker tweets/impartiality row. 2024 Huw Edwards criminal conviction. Evasion disproportionately prosecuted against women (~70% of convictions).

Scottish Child Payment.description: Devolved means-tested weekly benefit paid by Social Security Scotland to low-income families for each child under 16. Scotland's flagship anti-child-poverty measure — no UK equivalent. Stacks on top of Universal Credit / Tax Credits / Pension Credit.
Scottish Child Payment.legal_basis: Social Security (Scotland) Act 2018; Scottish Child Payment Regulations 2020; enabled by Scotland Act 2016 devolution of specified benefit powers
Scottish Child Payment.notes: Fraser of Allander Institute and IFS modelling suggests Scottish Child Payment is the single largest driver of Scotland's lower projected child poverty rate vs rUK, but the cost displaces spending elsewhere. Scottish Government missed its interim 2023-24 statutory child poverty target (relative poverty 26% vs 18% target). The Scottish Fiscal Commission has flagged it as a structural budget pressure.

Environment Agency.description: Non-departmental public body created in 1996 (Environment Act 1995). Regulator and operator responsible for flood & coastal risk management in England, water resources, environmental permitting, fisheries, contaminated land, and climate-adaptation advice.
Environment Agency.beneficiaries: ~5.7 million properties in flood-risk areas; rivers, estuaries and coasts; bathing-water users; ~19,000 permitted businesses
Environment Agency.legal_basis: Environment Act 1995 Part I; Water Resources Act 1991; Flood and Water Management Act 2010; Environmental Permitting Regulations 2016; Environment Act 2021
Environment Agency.notes: Sewage crisis — EA accused of under-enforcement: between 2016-2021 only 7 prosecutions vs tens of thousands of spills. OEP (Office for Environmental Protection) issued formal information notice to DEFRA/Ofwat/EA in 2023. EA budget for environmental-protection work fell ~50% real terms 2010-2020, correlating with declining river-quality monitoring. Water (Special Measures) Act 2025 gives EA power to block bonuses at failing firms and impose unlimited civil penalties.

DEPARTMENT OF HEALTH.notes: Scope note: the OSCAR £83B line is DHSC *net* of the Provider Sector branch — the full DHSC group headline is £181.7B (HM Treasury Main Estimates 2024-25). Biggest current story: **NHS England abolition**, announced by PM Starmer and Health Secretary Wes Streeting on **13 March 2025**. NHSE is merging back into DHSC over ~2 years, with a combined headcount cut of ~50% (~9,000–10,000 posts). It is the biggest NHS commissioning reorganisation since the 2012 Lansley reforms that established NHSE in the first place. The Institute for Government, King's Fund and Nuffield Trust all warned this absorbs management bandwidth precisely when waiting lists and productivity need focus. Resident-doctor strikes ran 44 days through 2023-24; the September 2024 deal (~22.3% over 2 years) closed that dispute but a new 2025-26 ballot reopened it. The **Leng Review (July 2025)** on Physician Associate scope of practice recommended renaming to 'Physician Assistant' and pausing expansion.

HOME OFFICE.description: The UK's domestic security ministry. Funds the 43 territorial police forces via grant-in-aid, runs Border Force and UK Visas & Immigration, administers the asylum system, coordinates counter-terrorism policing, and oversees passports, drugs and fire policy. Small-boats and asylum hotels dominate its public profile since 2022.
HOME OFFICE.beneficiaries: UK residents protected by 147,746 police officers · ~175,000 people in asylum support · ~3 million visa/settlement applications / year · ~7 million passports issued / year
HOME OFFICE.legal_basis: Police Act 1996; Police Reform and Social Responsibility Act 2011; Immigration and Asylum Act 1999; Nationality and Borders Act 2022; Illegal Migration Act 2023 (being repealed); Safety of Rwanda Act 2024 (being repealed); National Security Act 2023

HOME OFFICE.notes: The **Rwanda Migration and Economic Development Partnership** was cancelled on **6 July 2024** — PM Starmer's second full day in office. Total sunk cost ~£700M for zero enforced removals (NAO March 2024 investigation). The **Border Security, Asylum and Immigration Bill 2025** replaces it: creates a statutory Border Security Command, new offences targeting smuggling-gang supply chains, and repeals most of the Safety of Rwanda Act 2024 and Illegal Migration Act 2023. **Bibby Stockholm barge** operated at Portland from Aug 2023 to Nov 2024 — Legionella bacteria detected within days of the first arrivals; Albanian asylum-seeker **Leonard Farruku died by suicide onboard in December 2023**. **Manston processing centre** was catastrophically overcrowded Oct–Nov 2022 (4,000 people in a 1,600-capacity site, diphtheria outbreak, one detainee death). On policing: the **Casey Review (March 2023)** declared the Met institutionally racist, misogynistic and homophobic, following the Sarah Everard murder by serving officer Wayne Couzens (March 2021) and the David Carrick serial-rapist case (Jan 2023). The **Angiolini Inquiry Part 1 report (Feb 2024)** concluded Couzens should never have been a police officer — vetting reforms now rolling out across forces. Despite ~£700M spent on Rwanda deterrence and multiple legislative packages, the 2024 small-boats total set a new record.

DEPARTMENT FOR EDUCATION.description: England's third-largest spending department. Funds schools (via LAs and academy trusts), SEND provision, early years, 16-19 education, apprenticeships, higher-education regulation, student loans, and teacher pensions. Money reaches schools through two channels: Dedicated Schools Grant ring-fenced to LAs, and ESFA direct grants to academy trusts (now 82% of secondary pupils, 42% of primary).
DEPARTMENT FOR EDUCATION.beneficiaries: ~8.2M pupils in state-funded schools · ~2.86M HE students · ~339,580 apprenticeship starts / year · ~1.3M children in funded early-years · ~468,400 FTE teachers
DEPARTMENT FOR EDUCATION.legal_basis: Education Act 1996; School Standards and Framework Act 1998; Academies Act 2010; Children and Families Act 2014 Part 3 (SEND); Higher Education and Research Act 2017; Skills and Post-16 Education Act 2022

DEPARTMENT FOR EDUCATION.notes: Scope note: the £140B OSCAR line is total DfE departmental spending including student loan outlay scored via the RAB charge — not all of this is cash spending in the public-perception sense. Biggest story: IFS Annual Report on Education Spending 2024 found **real-terms per-pupil funding in state schools only returned to its 2010 level in 2024-25** — a lost decade. **SEND financial crisis**: NAO (Oct 2024) branded the system 'financially unsustainable'; LA DSG deficits ~£3.2B cumulative with the statutory override expiring March 2026 and no replacement policy. The **98% SEND tribunal overturn rate** is repeatedly cited by the Education Select Committee as evidence LAs routinely refuse statutorily-owed support. **Plan 5 student loans** (Aug 2023) cut the threshold £27,295→£25,000 and extended the term 30→40 years — IFS calculated this shifts ~£2.3B/year from taxpayers to graduates, hitting middle earners hardest (regressive relative to Plan 2). **Ruth Perry Prevention of Future Deaths report (7 December 2023)** by the Senior Coroner for Berkshire found that Ofsted's inspection 'likely contributed' to the headteacher's death; Ofsted's **single-phrase overall-effectiveness judgements were abolished on 2 September 2024**. University sector stress: OfS May 2024 found ~40% of English HE providers forecast a deficit in 2024-25, compounded by the January 2024 dependant-visa ban collapsing international postgraduate numbers.

MINISTRY OF HOUSING, COMMUNITIES AND LOC.notes: Renamed from DLUHC to MHCLG in July 2024 under the Starmer government. **Birmingham s114 (5 September 2023) is the largest council bankruptcy in UK history** — £760M equal-pay liability plus a £131M Oracle ERP implementation disaster, triggering a 21% council tax rise over two years and ~£300M in forced asset sales. LGIU's March 2024 survey found 51% of councils 'not confident' of balancing 2024-25 budgets; a quarter of district councils risk s114 by 2026 if the DSG SEND deficit statutory override expires as scheduled (March 2026). **Temporary-accommodation cliff**: London boroughs alone spend ~£4M/day on TA (up 68% in two years). LHA subsidy frozen at 2011 rates forces councils to absorb ~£700M/year gap. LHA was restored to 30th percentile in April 2024 at ~£1.2B/year cost, then **re-frozen from April 2025** after just 12 months — Crisis and Shelter estimate this will push a further 80,000 households into housing stress. **Grenfell Tower Inquiry Phase 2 Final Report published 4 September 2024** with 58 recommendations including a single construction-industry regulator. **Awaab's Law** regulations (following the 2020 death of two-year-old Awaab Ishak in Rochdale from damp/mould) commencing 2025-26 force social landlords to fix damp within strict timeframes. NAO and PAC criticised political steering of Levelling Up Fund rounds — 2022 allocations disproportionately benefited Conservative-held constituencies per IFS analysis. Real-terms council funding still ~10% below 2010 per capita despite 2024-25 Core Spending Power uplift.

Academies - Pre 16.notes: Scope note: this node is £28.1B GROSS pre-16 direct grant. In the tree you'll also see 'DfE Grants to Academies Offset' at −£37.0B — that's NOT a funding cut; it's the recoupment from local-authority Dedicated Schools Grant so the same money isn't counted twice. When a pupil moves from a maintained school to an academy, the LA's DSG is reduced by that pupil's NFF entitlement and ESFA pays the academy directly instead. Critical controversy: **Multi-Academy Trust CEO pay** became a political flashpoint after IfG / Observer investigations showed ~100 trust CEOs earning >£150k in 2022-23; six trusts paid CEOs over £250k. The Education Select Committee (2023) called for pay restraint. Academy failures: **Wakefield City Academies Trust collapsed in 2017** after stripping ~£1M from reserves before handing schools back. **Bright Tribe Trust** lost its 10 schools in 2018 after NAO found governance failures. The regulator ESFA issues **Financial Notices to Improve (FNtIs)** to academies running deficits — ~40 active at any time. Academy freedoms over teacher pay/conditions: in theory academies can diverge from the School Teachers' Pay and Conditions Document (STPCD); in practice ~95% still follow it because they hire from the same teacher labour market. The **2022 Schools White Paper** aim of 'every school in a strong MAT by 2030' was dropped by Labour in 2024.

DfE Grants to Academies Offset.description: Accounting mechanism, NOT a funding cut. When a maintained school becomes an academy, the Education & Skills Funding Agency pays the trust directly — but the local authority's Dedicated Schools Grant would otherwise still include that pupil's funding. This −£37B line recoups the LA DSG by the same amount so the same money isn't counted twice. Visually it appears as a huge negative, which is why it confuses readers — but it's a bookkeeping contra-entry, not real spending.
DfE Grants to Academies Offset.beneficiaries: Taxpayers (prevents double-counting in public finance totals); ultimately the same academy pupils funded by the Academies gross line.
DfE Grants to Academies Offset.legal_basis: Academies Act 2010 (s.14 — recoupment of local authority funding); Academies (Recoupment) Regulations 2013

key_stats.value: ~£3.5B (the net new money central gov is directing to academies, above what would have flowed to LAs anyway)

key_stats.label: Mechanism

DfE Grants to Academies Offset.notes: This line is a perennial source of confusion for readers. Public commentary sometimes cites the gross £40B 'Academies' figure as 'cost of academies' without netting the offset — that's misleading. The real *net* central-government spending specifically attributable to academies (above what would have gone to LAs anyway) is ~£3.5B, mostly transition costs, capital for academy openings, Regional Schools Commissioners, ESFA running costs, and specific academy-only programmes (e.g. free school establishment). Accountants call this a 'netting-off' or 'matched flow' and it's standard practice under the HM Treasury Fiscal Framework. The Education Select Committee and IfG have repeatedly asked DfE to present academy spending net of offset in headline communications.

MINISTRY OF JUSTICE.notes: **Prison-capacity crisis + SDS40**: PM Starmer's Lord Chancellor Shabana Mahmood signed the statutory instrument moving automatic release from 50% to 40% of sentence effective **10 September 2024** — an emergency response to the 88,521 peak population (6 Sept 2024) leaving <1% headroom. Operation Early Dawn (holding remand prisoners in police cells) was triggered multiple times late 2024. **Gauke Independent Sentencing Review** (commissioned Dec 2024; final report May 2025) proposes: (1) an intermediate court tier between Magistrates' and Crown, (2) presumption against short custodial sentences, (3) 'earned progression' release model, (4) IPP residual cohort reforms. **HMP Wandsworth escape** — Daniel Khalife (ex-soldier, terrorism-charge defendant) absconded clinging to underside of a food-delivery lorry **6 September 2023**; recaptured days later. HMI Probation has repeatedly rated **no Probation Service region 'Good'** in recent annual reports; multiple Probation Delivery Units rated Inadequate. **LASPO 2012** withdrew civil legal aid from most housing, welfare, family and immigration cases — sustained criticism from Bach Commission, Westminster Commission and Justice Committee; directly linked to rise in Litigants in Person in family courts. **Prison self-harm incidents at record levels** in 2023-24 (HMPPS Safety in Custody Statistics). **HMCTS Reform cost overruns**: NAO and PAC critical of scope reduction alongside £375M → £1.3B+ budget growth. **IPP residual ~2,700**: UN Special Rapporteur and Justice Committee have repeatedly called for resentencing of prisoners still detained under the 2012-abolished Imprisonment for Public Protection sentence.

HM TREASURY.notes: **Truss-Kwarteng mini-budget crisis**: 23 September 2022 'Growth Plan' announced £45B of unfunded tax cuts (top-rate abolition, NI reversal, stamp duty cuts) with no OBR forecast published. 30-year gilt yield rose ~120 basis points in three sessions; sterling hit record low $1.035. LDI (liability-driven investment) pension schemes faced margin calls on interest-rate swaps triggering a forced-selling doom loop in long-dated gilts. On 28 Sept, BoE launched a temporary targeted gilt-buying facility up to £65B capacity (actual purchases ~£19.3B) to stabilise LDI funds. Kwarteng sacked 14 Oct; **Truss resigned 20 Oct — shortest-serving PM in UK history (49 days)**. Hunt reversed virtually all measures by 17 Oct but higher debt-service bill was baked into forward curves (~£20-30B extra over the medium term). **Index-linked gilt shock 2022-23**: RPI peaked at 14.2% October 2022. Because ~25% of gilts are RPI-linked, coupons and principal auto-uplift — OBR estimated **~£50B of additional debt-interest crystallised in 2022-23 alone** from the inflation spike. This is why UK debt interest rose faster than any other G7 country's. **Oct 2024 Budget fiscal rule reform**: Chancellor Reeves switched the debt target from PSND to PSND ex-BoE (excludes APF/QT losses; counts illiquid financial assets) — creating ~£50B of additional investment headroom. The IFS Green Budget 2024 makes the case that debt-interest 'crowding out' is the binding fiscal constraint. NAO and Treasury Select Committee have questioned the pace of BoE's active gilt sales (QT) given realised-loss crystallisation.

DEPARTMENT FOR TRANSPORT.notes: **HS2 Phase 2 cancellation (4 October 2023)** at the Conservative Party conference by PM Sunak: Birmingham-Manchester and the eastern leg scrapped; £36B 'Network North' reallocation announced for unspecified road/bus/rail schemes. PAC (Feb 2024) called HS2 'a casebook example of how not to run a major project'. Reporting alleged Sunak announced without full Cabinet sign-off — Midlands + Northern Conservative mayors (Andy Street, Ben Houchen) publicly objected. **Rail nationalisation**: Passenger Railway Services (Public Ownership) Act received Royal Assent November 2024 — **South Western Railway became the first operator transferred to the public-sector operator (DfT Operator) on 25 May 2025**. Full Great British Railways Bill expected in 2025 to consolidate track + train under a single guiding mind. **Bus £2 → £3 cap** from 1 January 2025 — a controversial Labour Budget Oct 2024 decision, extended through end of 2025. **Silvertown Tunnel** opened **7 April 2025** (tolled) — first new Thames road crossing in east London since the Blackwall Tunnel. **A303 Stonehenge tunnel**: quashed by High Court 2021, re-approved 2023, **cancelled by Labour July 2024** with ~£166M sunk costs. **Smart motorways scandal**: coroner rulings into fatalities on All-Lane-Running sections + BBC Panorama investigations drove the April 2023 cancellation; campaigners continue to call for hard-shoulder reinstatement on existing sections. **TfL Khan-Shapps feud** through 2022-24 over Covid bailout conditions, TfL capital funding and ULEZ expansion (Aug 2023) to outer London — ULEZ cited as a factor in the 2023 Uxbridge by-election.

DEPARTMENT FOR ENERGY SECURITY AND NET Z.description: UK department created 7 February 2023 when the Sunak government split BEIS. Scope: energy security, decarbonisation + climate policy, Contracts for Difference (CfD) renewables subsidies, Nuclear Decommissioning Authority (including Sellafield), nuclear new-build (Hinkley Point C · Sizewell C · SMRs via Great British Nuclear), Energy Bills Support schemes (wound down), and sponsorship of Great British Energy + Ofgem + Low Carbon Contracts Company.
DEPARTMENT FOR ENERGY SECURITY AND NET Z.beneficiaries: All GB electricity + gas consumers (EBSS rebates 2022-23; standing-charge levies) · offshore wind + solar + tidal developers · ~11,000 Sellafield staff + EDF Hinkley C workforce (~10,000 at peak) · ~3.5M fuel-poor households via Warm Home Discount · Aberdeen supply chain + Crown Estate partnership via GB Energy
DEPARTMENT FOR ENERGY SECURITY AND NET Z.legal_basis: Energy Act 2013 (CfD regime) · Energy Act 2023 (hydrogen + CCUS + Ofgem net-zero duty) · Energy Act 2004 (NDA creation) · Nuclear Installations Act 1965 · Climate Change Act 2008 (statutory net-zero 2050) · Energy Prices Act 2022 (EBSS/EPG emergency powers) · Great British Energy Act 2024

DEPARTMENT FOR ENERGY SECURITY AND NET Z.notes: **AR5 offshore wind disaster (September 2023)**: DESNZ refused to raise the £44/MWh administrative strike price despite unanimous industry warnings from RWE / Ørsted / SSE / Iberdrola / Vattenfall about post-Ukraine-invasion supply-chain inflation. **Zero offshore wind bids cleared** — a policy embarrassment that delayed 2030 pipeline by at least a year. AR6 had to be fundamentally re-parameterised with higher admin strike + ring-fenced offshore pot, which worked: 9.6 GW awarded. **Sellafield** is 'repeatedly over budget and late' (NAO July 2024): SIXEP Continuity Plant ~6 years late + ~£1B over budget; Box Encapsulation Plant 17 years late; £122M taxpayer settlement in 2018 after Supreme Court-confirmed procurement breach on Magnox; 2023 Guardian 'Nuclear Leaks' investigation raised cyber + workforce-culture concerns. **EBSS value-for-money critique** (NAO March 2024): universal £400 rebate 'not well targeted' — went to high-income households regardless of need. **Hinkley Point C cost** has risen from ~£18B (2015 prices at FID) to EDF's current £31-46B range (2024 money), with first power slipping to 2029-2031 — costs borne by EDF/CGN equity under CfD but delays risk 2030 clean-power target. **Sizewell C** uses Regulated Asset Base model, shifting construction-risk cost onto consumer bills — contentious precedent from Nuclear Energy (Financing) Act 2022.

DEPARTMENT FOR CULTURE, MEDIA AND SPORT.description: UK department for arts, heritage, sport, gambling regulation, civil society, creative industries, and cultural aspects of digital policy. After the February 2023 split, most telecoms + AI + digital-infrastructure functions moved to DSIT; DCMS retained creative industries, cultural digital and media. **Scope note**: the department's own spend is ~£9B — NOT to be confused with 'DCMS sectors GVA' (~£125B, 6% of UK GVA) which is an economic-footprint statistic.
DEPARTMENT FOR CULTURE, MEDIA AND SPORT.beneficiaries: ~24.5M TV Licence-holding households funding the BBC · ~985 Arts Council England NPOs (2023-26) · 16 DCMS-sponsored national museums (~50M+ visits/year pre-pandemic) · ~22M UK adult gamblers regulated by Gambling Commission · ~400,000 listed buildings + ~20,000 scheduled monuments under Historic England · ~2.4M jobs in creative industries
DEPARTMENT FOR CULTURE, MEDIA AND SPORT.legal_basis: Communications Act 2003 (BBC + Ofcom framework) · Wireless Telegraphy Act 2006 (licence-fee enforcement, s.363 criminal offence) · BBC Royal Charter 2017-2027 · Museums and Galleries Act 1992 · National Lottery etc. Act 1993 · Gambling Act 2005 · Ancient Monuments and Archaeological Areas Act 1979 · Planning (Listed Buildings and Conservation Areas) Act 1990

DEPARTMENT FOR CULTURE, MEDIA AND SPORT.notes: **BBC Charter expires 31 December 2027**: DCMS launched Funding Model Review November 2024 examining alternatives — subscription, hybrid, household levy (like Germany's €18.36/month Rundfunkbeitrag), advertising, general taxation. Full privatisation ruled out. Decriminalisation of licence-fee evasion consulted 2020 but not enacted. **Licence-fee evasion prosecutions disproportionately female**: ~70% of single-justice-procedure TV licence convictions are of women (MoJ data) — long-standing concern flagged by Commons Justice Committee. **ENO relocation row (2022-24)**: ACE required English National Opera to leave London (final destination Manchester, £17M/yr → £12.8M transitional). **Oldham Coliseum closed March 2023** after ACE withdrew NPO status. 2023 'content restrictions' letter from then-SoS Lucy Frazer warning NPOs against 'political statements' widely condemned as chilling effect on artistic expression. Per-capita ACE spend outside London ~£11.70 vs London ~£14.66 (was £21 vs £7 in 2017 baseline). **Gambling Act review White Paper April 2023 — implementation through 2024-25**: online slot stake limits £5/spin (adults 25+, Sept 2024) and £2/spin (18-24, Feb 2025) · statutory levy on operators (~1% GGY) replacing voluntary RET · affordability checks piloted but softened post-2024 election amid horseracing industry pushback. **Gary Lineker** impartiality rows 2023 + 2024 ending with announced MOTD departure end of 2024-25 season. **Huw Edwards** criminal conviction 2024 for accessing indecent images of children. **National Lottery transition Feb 2024**: Allwyn replaced Camelot as operator — initial revenue dip caused ~£200-300M drop in good-cause distributions vs forecast, directly impacting ACE + Sport England + Heritage Fund.

DEPARTMENT FOR SCIENCE, INNOVATION AND T.description: UK department created 7 February 2023 when the Sunak government split BEIS into four successor departments — DSIT was designed to ring-fence R&D + digital + tech policy. Inherits science and research from BEIS; digital and telecoms from former DCMS; and (from November 2023) absorbed the Government Digital Service (GDS), Central Digital and Data Office (CDDO) and Incubator for AI (i.AI) from the Cabinet Office. Sponsors UKRI + AI Security Institute + UK Space Agency + Alan Turing Institute.
DEPARTMENT FOR SCIENCE, INNOVATION AND T.beneficiaries: 157 universities + research institutes (REF 2021) · ~22,000 UKRI-funded PhD students · 10,000+ SMEs per year via Innovate UK + Catapults + KTPs · UK AI frontier ecosystem (DeepMind, Anthropic UK, Cohere) · ~52,000 UK space sector jobs · rural + urban telecoms consumers via Project Gigabit
DEPARTMENT FOR SCIENCE, INNOVATION AND T.legal_basis: Higher Education and Research Act 2017 (created UKRI + OfS) · Online Safety Act 2023 (Ofcom-enforced children's + illegal-harms duties) · Space Industry Act 2018 · Communications Act 2003 · National Security and Investment Act 2021 (mandatory screening of foreign investment in 17 sensitive sectors inc. AI + semiconductors) · Digital Economy Acts 2010 & 2017

DEPARTMENT FOR SCIENCE, INNOVATION AND T.notes: **Horizon Europe rejoining (January 2024)** restored UK association after 3 post-Brexit years of 'associate-in-limbo'. UK researchers can again coordinate bids on the €95B programme; Copernicus association followed. Net contributor/recipient balance won't be clear until programme closes (2027). **Nurse Review (March 2023)** by Sir Paul Nurse recommended simplifying UKRI structure — UKRI reorganised in 2024 with new 'Impact, Engagement and Place' function; Strategic Priorities Fund wound down. **AI Safety Institute → AI Security Institute (February 2025)**: Labour's first DSIT reshuffle under Peter Kyle narrowed the institute's formal mandate, renamed it, and added a Criminal Misuse Unit. Summit sequence: Bletchley (Nov 2023) → Seoul (May 2024) → Paris AI Action Summit (Feb 2025) → India AI Impact Summit (Feb 2026). Civil-society groups (Ada Lovelace Institute, Connected by Data) criticised the narrowing of scope away from broader societal harms. **Online Safety Act 2023 children's duties live July 2025**; Ofcom issued first enforcement notices Q4 2025. **Semiconductor strategy inadequacy**: Commons S&T Committee + techUK consistently called the £1B/10yr an order of magnitude too small. Labour Oct 2024 Budget added only modest new funding (~£50-100M for South Wales compound semiconductors). **EDI / 'decolonise' funding controversy (2023-24)**: Conservative science minister Michelle Donelan publicly pressured UKRI over EDI Advisory Group membership October 2023 ('Donelan letter' episode) — triggered a £15,000 libel settlement paid from public funds to an affected academic in March 2024. Labour partially restored the approach post-July 2024. **Alan Turing Institute 'Turing 2.0' review (2024-25)**: significant restructuring, staff reductions, refocus on defence + health + environment missions. **Ottoline Leyser UKRI CEO departed summer 2024** amid reorganisation stress.

DEPARTMENT FOR ENVIRONMENT, FOOD AND RUR.description: UK department responsible for environmental protection, food + farming, fisheries, rural communities and biodiversity in England (devolved administrations handle most policy directly elsewhere). Funds core DEFRA + arm's-length bodies: Environment Agency (EA — environmental regulation + flood defence), Natural England (protected sites + nature recovery), Rural Payments Agency, Forestry Commission, Marine Management Organisation, Animal + Plant Health Agency. Post-Brexit DEFRA runs the UK's farm-payments regime (ELM replacing EU CAP), UK REACH chemicals regulation, and the statutory Environmental Improvement Plan.
DEPARTMENT FOR ENVIRONMENT, FOOD AND RUR.beneficiaries: ~82,000 English farm businesses receiving direct + ELM payments · ~5.7M properties in flood-risk areas covered by EA programmes · UK fishing industry (~11,000 licensed fishers + ~5,500 vessels) · ~4,100 SSSIs covering ~1.1M hectares · ~1,500 designated bathing waters + ~40,000 km monitored rivers · forestry sector + 3M+ ha UK woodland · ~17% of English population in rural communities
DEPARTMENT FOR ENVIRONMENT, FOOD AND RUR.legal_basis: Water Resources Act 1991 (EA water management) · Environment Act 1995 (created EA) · Flood and Water Management Act 2010 · Environmental Permitting Regulations 2016 · Agriculture Act 2020 (ELM statutory basis) · Environment Act 2021 (OEP + EIP + legally binding targets) · Water (Special Measures) Act 2025

DEPARTMENT FOR ENVIRONMENT, FOOD AND RUR.notes: **Sewage crisis is the defining DEFRA story**: 464,056 storm-overflow events in 2023 (up 54% on 2022, partly reflecting EDM coverage going near-100% vs ~91% in 2022). All 11 English wastewater companies under joint EA-Ofwat investigation — the largest-ever criminal investigation in the sector. The **Office for Environmental Protection** issued a formal information notice to DEFRA / Ofwat / EA in 2023 finding **possible breaches of law** in how storm-overflow regulations had been interpreted for decades. **Water (Special Measures) Act 2025 (February 2025)**: gives Ofwat power to block executive bonuses at failing water firms, introduces automatic civil penalties under civil standard of proof, raises fine ceilings, mandates independent monitoring of every storm overflow — first major water-industry enforcement reform in a generation. **Thames Water crisis (June 2024 onwards)**: ~16M customers · ~£19B debt · £1B+ annual losses · narrowly avoided Special Administration Regime via court-approved £3B emergency debt package + equity raise. Restructuring ongoing. **Inheritance Tax / Agricultural Property Relief reform (Autumn Budget 2024)**: from April 2026, agricultural + business assets above combined £1M threshold face 20% effective IHT (half standard 40%). Treasury claims ~500 estates/year affected; NFU claims up to ~70,000 farms exposed over time. **IFS analysis found majority of prior relief value accrued to the largest estates**. Thousands of farmers protested Whitehall 19 November 2024, with rolling tractor protests through 2025. **SFI 2024 paused 11 March 2025** — DEFRA closed to new applications with effectively no notice after the £2.4B annual budget ceiling hit faster than modelled; sector outcry from farmers mid-transition from BPS. **ClientEarth NO2 litigation**: DEFRA repeatedly lost ClientEarth cases (2015, 2016, 2018) over failure to meet air-quality limits — remains live regulatory issue. **Bovine TB badger cull**: long-running controversy; Labour 2024 manifesto committed to phase-out — transition contested.

2.1 Military defence.notes: **Equipment Plan 2023-2033 unaffordable (NAO Dec 2023)**: budgeted funding £305.5B against forecast costs £322.4B = **£16.9B shortfall** — first time NAO declared the Plan unaffordable. Plan total £288.6B. Nuclear + Navy portfolios worst-affected. **Defence Nuclear Enterprise**: lifetime forecast £118.5B over 10 years — a £38.2B single-year jump vs 2022-32 plan (largest single driver of Plan unaffordability). **Dreadnought SSBN programme**: lifetime £31B + £10B contingency (2015 baseline, now being pressure-tested). CASD (Continuous At-Sea Deterrent) unbroken since 1969. **Strategic Defence Review June 2025** (Starmer first major review): ~62 recommendations ALL accepted — pivot to autonomous/uncrewed systems · munitions stockpile rebuild · digital targeting web · NATO-first posture. **Ajax armoured vehicle**: £5.5B contract with General Dynamics UK · years of delay + noise/vibration injuries to crew during trials · Initial Operating Capability declared July 2025 after ~a decade of slippage. **Recruitment crisis**: Capita £495M RPP consistently missed Army targets · FY23-24 intake 10,930 vs outflow 16,260 (net -5,330) · net outflow every year since 2016 · new tri-service Armed Forces Recruiting Service contract awarded 2024. **Service Family Accommodation** chronic housing-quality complaints under now-replaced CarillionAmey/VIVO contracts. 7.A Medical services.description: Devolved health services across the UK's three non-England nations. Each has an INTEGRATED model (no purchaser-provider split like NHS England): NHS Scotland runs 14 territorial Health Boards + 7 national special boards; NHS Wales runs 7 Local Health Boards + 3 trusts; Northern Ireland uniquely INTEGRATES health + social care in 5 HSC Trusts (not 'NHS', branded 'HSC' since 1973). All three free at point of use with free prescriptions.

7.A Medical services.notes: **Audit Scotland February 2025** concluded NHS Scotland is **'not financially sustainable'** — 7 of 14 territorial boards required Scottish Government brokerage/loans in 2024-25 (up from 4 prior year). Scottish Covid-19 Inquiry running 2023-26 separate from UK Inquiry. **NHS Wales**: Betsi Cadwaladr placed in special measures Feb 2023 (previously 2015-2020) after the 2022-23 vascular services crisis at Ysbyty Glan Clwyd — HIW + RCS England reviews found 'significant patient safety concerns' + multiple avoidable deaths. De-escalated to 'targeted intervention' June 2024. Dec 2024 'New Deal' pay + productivity package. **NI HSC**: uniquely integrates health with social care in 5 Trusts — means social-care backlog + hospital-discharge pressures compound within a single budget line. NIAO *Major Health Care Waiting Times* (2023) called performance 'unsustainable decline'. HSC Board abolished 2022 — commissioning moved to Department of Health's Strategic Planning and Performance Group (SPPG). Nurses' RCN strike December 2019 was the first RCN strike in its 103-year history. Stormont restored Feb 2024 after 2-year suspension; Health Minister Mike Nesbitt (UUP) launched 2024-25 Elective Care Framework including ~£60M+ cross-border referrals (Dublin + GB) + expanded private commissioning.

Financial Assistance To Other Institutio.description: HM Treasury's accounting bucket for cash flows to non-government bodies where HMT acts as sovereign backstop. In 2024-25 dominated by **quarterly indemnity payments to the Bank of England's Asset Purchase Facility (BEAPFF)** covering BoE's losses on unwinding the QE gilt portfolio. Smaller flows from Covid loan-guarantee calls (BBLS/CBILS/CLBILS), energy Supplier-of-Last-Resort costs (Bulb), UK Asset Resolution runoff (Northern Rock / Bradford & Bingley legacy), National Wealth Fund capitalisation, and Ukraine ERA loan commitments. Line was near-zero in pre-2020 OSCAR vintages — exploded with Covid + QT reversal.

Financial Assistance To Other Institutio.notes: **CRITICAL SCOPE NOTE**: Exact £ decomposition of the £71B is NOT published in any single public table — the ~£28-30B APF-in-2024-25 estimate is a differenced figure from the cumulative £85.9B since October 2022. Treat as estimate. **The APF indemnity is scored as AME spending, not as debt interest in the National Accounts** — should NOT double-count with the separate Debt Interest Payments tree line. Sanity check against ONS PSF 'Interest payable' (MF6U series). **Truss mini-budget Sept 2022** triggered BoE's emergency gilt-buying (via APF) that stabilised the LDI crisis — those gilts are still being unwound under QT, generating the losses this bucket covers. **BBLS fraud scandal**: NAO £4.9B fraud estimate + Lord Agnew resignation January 2022 over fraud-control failures. **Bulb SoLR**: the hand-over to Octopus is under PAC scrutiny over whether the repayment structure captures true value. **Treasury Committee 2024** questioned whether the Bank's active gilt-sales pace is taxpayer-optimal given faster unwinding crystallises losses sooner. **G7 context**: US Fed remittances to Treasury also went negative (deferred asset) in 2022-23, but the UK's APF indemnity is structurally unique (cash-settled, not accrual-deferred). Critics argue this COFOG 4.1 line is a catch-all that obscures what is effectively a monetary-policy flow inside fiscal accounts.

NHS Commissioning Board (NHS England).description: NHS England (operating name of the NHS Commissioning Board) is the DHSC arm's-length body that allocates funds to 42 Integrated Care Boards, directly commissions specialised + primary care, and sets national standards. Created 1 October 2012 by Health and Social Care Act 2012 to give the NHS operational independence from ministers. **13 March 2025: PM Starmer + Health Secretary Streeting announced NHSE will be abolished and merged back into DHSC over ~2 years** — biggest NHS reorganisation since the 2012 reforms that created it.

NHS Commissioning Board (NHS England).notes: **Biggest reorganisation since Lansley 2012 reforms — which NHSE itself embodied**. Rationale: re-centralise political accountability for NHS performance with ministers, end 2012's 'arm's length' settlement. Kings Fund / IfG / Nuffield Trust all warned that a 2-year reorg absorbs senior management attention during a period of record elective waiting lists (~7.4M referrals late 2024) + productivity push — comparing with the 2012 reforms' 3 'lost years'. Redundancy costs ~£50-100k per senior post (NAO 2016 methodology) — payback period on £500M/year savings likely 2-3 years before net. Pending primary legislation, NHSE continues as statutory body; functions transfer operationally first, legally later. **Accountability concern**: concerns from clinical bodies + select committees that re-absorbing NHSE into DHSC without clear operational firewall risks politicising operational decisions (waiting-list targets, service closures). **CARAN allocation fairness debate**: longstanding concern (Health Foundation) that formula under-weights deprivation vs age — 2016 ACRA refresh added health-inequalities adjustment but critics argue it's too small. **Specialised commissioning phased delegation** to ICBs since 2023-24 criticised for postcode-variation risk in low-volume services — abolition adds further structural uncertainty.

MHCLG Local Government.description: The grant-routing sub-line of MHCLG — principal conduit through which central government channels revenue + specific-purpose funding to England's 317 principal local authorities. Sits alongside (and is quantitatively larger than) the 'Communities' policy side. Controls Social Care Grant, pooled Better Care Fund, residual Revenue Support Grant, Section 31 pass-through grants, Levelling Up/Towns/UKSPF programmes. Does NOT control council-tax or retained business rates — those are local — but sets the rules, the settlement, and top-up grants that complete 'Core Spending Power' (CSP).

MHCLG Local Government.notes: **s114 contagion 2018-2023** exposed structural under-funding + risk-taking: Northamptonshire (2018) · Croydon (2020/2022/2023) · Slough (2021) · Thurrock (2022) · Woking (2023) · Birmingham (Sept 2023) · Nottingham (Nov 2023). Woking's £1.9B debt on ~£2B of commercial property is the most egregious single case; Birmingham's equal-pay liabilities (Abdulla v Birmingham CC line) + botched Oracle ERP implementation (>£100M overspend) is the largest council collapse in UK history. **Commissioners are in place** at Birmingham, Nottingham, Thurrock, Woking and Slough. **LGA, SIGOMA, County Councils Network, IFS, NAO, PAC** all repeatedly flag that grant-routing through MHCLG has been systemically insufficient to match statutory duties — especially adult social care, SEND, temporary accommodation — forcing councils into reserve-depletion and commercial risk. **Local-audit crisis**: ~99% of 2022-23 LA accounts were late as of 2024; MHCLG statutory backstop (Sept 2024 for 2022-23) forced mass 'disclaimed' opinions. **Household Support Fund**: persistently 'temporary' since Oct 2021, renewed successively in each fiscal event at £742-842M.

MHCLG Communities.notes: **Grenfell Tower Inquiry Phase 2 Final Report (4 September 2024)** identified 'decades of failure by central government' including DCLG (MHCLG's predecessor), naming specific officials and ministers. 58 recommendations include single construction-products regulator, single social-housing regulator, college of fire + rescue, chief construction adviser. Scathing findings on **Arconic, Kingspan, Celotex, Rydon, Studio E, Kensington & Chelsea TMO, LFB** and successive governments. Deputy PM Angela Rayner formal gov response published Feb 2025 accepting majority of recommendations. **Remediation pace is the live operational controversy**: 9 years after the fire, the majority of identified unsafe buildings remain not-remediated; leaseholders face interim safety costs (waking watches, rocketing insurance); Building Safety Levy timeline slipped repeatedly. **LHA re-freeze April 2025** after 12-month unfreeze was criticised by Shelter / Crisis / JRF / IFS as actively worsening the TA crisis. **Construction products enforcement**: Arconic + Kingspan + Celotex placed under review post-Phase 2; MHCLG consulting on new products regulator 2024-25.

Department of Health (NHS).notes: **Infected Blood Inquiry final report (Sir Brian Langstaff, 20 May 2024)**: concluded contamination of NHS blood products in the 1970s-90s was **'not an accident'** — DHSC + predecessors criticised for deliberate cover-up. Drove creation of IBCA as separate £11.8B tree line. **UKHSA restructure (Dec 2023-Jan 2024)**: shift to narrower 'health security' remit focused on pandemic preparedness + 100-Days-Mission vaccine readiness, following Module 1 of Covid Inquiry (published July 2024). **CQC post-Dash reset**: new leadership + single assessment framework review + DHSC GiA increased to support turnaround. **Nottingham maternity inquiry** is the largest review in NHS history — Donna Ockenden leading, launched Sept 2022, covers ~2,500 cases across 3 hospital sites. Report repeatedly delayed. **MHRA Yellow Card** + Covid-vaccine post-authorisation scrutiny = politically contested territory with ongoing Parliamentary debate on adverse-event transparency. **Dentistry Recovery Plan Feb 2024**: NAO + Health Select Committee both questioned deliverability — 40% of adults NOT seen by NHS dentist in 24 months to June 2024.

Nuclear Decommissioning Authority.description: Non-Departmental Public Body sponsored by DESNZ, created by Energy Act 2004, operational since 1 April 2005. Responsible for the safe + secure clean-up of the UK's 17 earliest civil nuclear sites, legacy fuel cycle management (Sellafield + Magnox closure), and long-term geological disposal of higher-activity radioactive waste. Group encompasses Sellafield Ltd (integrated 2016) · Magnox Ltd (12 reactor sites, in-house 2019) · Dounreay Site Restoration · Nuclear Waste Services (formed 2022 merging LLWR + RWM + NDA waste functions) · International Nuclear Services · Nuclear Transport Solutions.
Nuclear Decommissioning Authority.beneficiaries: ~17,000 staff across NDA estate + thousands more in nuclear supply chain · West Cumbria regional economy (Sellafield is UK's largest nuclear employer · ~11,000 staff) · future generations (intergenerational waste-management benefit) · GDF candidate-community host economies (Mid-Copeland · South-Copeland · Theddlethorpe) · UK tier-2/tier-3 nuclear contractors (civils · robotics · waste handling)

Nuclear Decommissioning Authority.notes: **NAO 'Progress at Sellafield' (July 2024)**: headline conclusion — 'repeatedly over budget and late' on most complex projects (SCP, BEP, SPRS). NDA accepted recommendations + published revised Sellafield Strategy. **Sellafield cyber + workforce-culture controversy**: Guardian 'Nuclear Leaks' investigation Dec 2023 alleged foreign-state cyber compromise (disputed by Sellafield Ltd + ONR public statements), 'toxic' workplace culture, and under-reporting → ONR placed Sellafield into **enhanced regulatory attention** on cyber-security → Sellafield Ltd pleaded guilty June 2024 to criminal charges under Nuclear Industries Security Regulations 2003 (2013-2019 period) → fined **£332,500 + ~£53,000 costs** at Westminster Magistrates' Court August 2024. **'One NDA' operating model (2022-24)**: Sellafield + Magnox + DSRL + NWS brought under tighter NDA group governance; shared services, common engineering, integrated waste strategy. **Magnox 2014 procurement fiasco**: NDA's evaluation was materially flawed → £122M taxpayer settlement to unsuccessful bidders. **GDF community search** politically contentious in Cumbria + Lincolnshire — volunteer-community consent model + long-term geology concerns. **Intergenerational cost risk**: HMT discount-rate changes can swing reported discounted liability by tens of £bn without any change to underlying physical task.

National Highways.notes: **Smart motorways scandal** is the defining controversy. (2020) + manslaughter referrals considered by South Yorkshire Police (not progressed to charges). Campaigners (Smart Motorways Kill · Claire Mercer) continue pressing for **hard-shoulder reinstatement** rather than just pause on new schemes. **ALR programme cancelled April 2023** (Sunak government) — 14 planned schemes dropped; existing smart motorways retained with additional emergency refuge areas + Stopped Vehicle Detection upgrades. **Labour July 2024 A303 cancellation**: £166M sunk costs written off — High Court had quashed the original 2020 DCO in 2021, re-approved 2023, then cancelled entirely. **RIS3 (2025-30)** proposals under Labour revision pending Spending Review outcome. Bristish Broadcasting Corporation.description: UK public service broadcaster operating under Royal Charter. Core public services (TV channels, radio networks, BBC News, iPlayer, BBC Sounds, BBC Online) funded principally by the TV licence fee. Additional streams: FCDO grant-in-aid for BBC World Service + BBC Monitoring · commercial revenues from BBC Studios (production + international distribution + UKTV). **SCOPE NOTE**: this £7.73B tree line does NOT reconcile cleanly to any single BBC-published aggregate — BBC group total income 2023-24 was £5.98B (incl. £2.2B commercial which is NOT Exchequer spend). The £7.73B likely reflects DCMS/HMT accounting treatment of the licence fee as a tax (ONS reclassification since 2006) + forecast uplifts. Editor flagged this scope ambiguity for verification against DCMS Main Estimates.
